passage:
Monday. Mr Nilesh marked Gurleen late by one minute and gave her a zero for the quiz, though two boys who walked in after her got to sit. She felt her jaw tighten. "Rules are rules," he said, and turned to the board.

Wednesday. He spent twenty minutes at her desk untangling how forces work on a ramp, until it finally clicked. Nobody else in school explained it like that. She hated how grateful she felt.

Friday. She waited until the room emptied. "Sir, on Monday the boys who came in after me weren't penalised. Could you tell me how the late rule works?" He frowned, then rubbed his forehead. "You're right. I'll count your quiz." She said thank you, and meant it, still a little sore, still a little in awe.

qa.q: On which day did Mr Nilesh explain the ramp problem to Gurleen?
qa.a: On Wednesday.

qa.q: What two feelings did Gurleen have about Mr Nilesh by Friday?
qa.a: Respect and resentment together. She was still a little sore about the zero yet also in awe of how well he taught her.

qa.q: Why was it wise for Gurleen to raise the late rule specifically rather than complain about the teacher in general?
qa.a: A specific, calm question about one unfair event gave him something clear to fix. He could agree without feeling attacked, and she kept the respect for what he taught. 🙂

qa.q: How might Mr Nilesh have felt when Gurleen spoke to him on Friday?
qa.a: Probably uncomfortable at first, since he frowned and rubbed his forehead. But he admitted she was right, so he seems willing to correct a mistake when it is put fairly.

grounding: A strict teacher is unfair once yet teaches well; the protagonist holds both and raises the unfair part specifically.

passage:
"Hafsa, you've been staring at that page for ten minutes."
"Noor apa, Mrs Kapoor gave me four out of ten on the essay. But she added up the rubric wrong. I told her, and she said, 'Object again and I'll make sure you fail the term.'"
"She said that? In those words?"
"Yes. Everyone heard."
"And what did you feel?"
"My hands went cold. I just said sorry. Now I feel like a coward."
"Being afraid to speak isn't weakness. Did you keep the paper?"
"Yes."
"Good. Write down the date and her words tonight. Then we tell Ammi. The school has a grievance process, and you use it."
Hafsa took a breath and slid the page into a folder.

qa.q: What did Mrs Kapoor say she would do if Hafsa objected again?
qa.a: She said she would make sure Hafsa fails the term.

qa.q: What was Hafsa feeling after she said sorry to Mrs Kapoor, and what shows it?
qa.a: Fear and some shame about giving in. Her hands went cold and she called herself a coward.

qa.q: What steps does Noor suggest Hafsa take?
qa.a: Keep the paper, write down the date and Mrs Kapoor's words tonight, tell Ammi, and use the school's grievance process.

qa.q: How might Noor see Hafsa's silence in class?
qa.a: As understandable, not cowardly. She tells Hafsa that being afraid to speak is not weakness, and helps her find a safe way to be heard.

grounding: A teacher threatens failing marks for objecting; the protagonist is guided to keep records, tell a parent and use the grievance process.

passage:
Teacher's note, March.

While rechecking last term's science papers for the moderation meeting, I found that I had mis-added Vaibhav's total in November. He had asked me about it then and I had brushed him off. I called him in and said plainly that the mistake was mine and that his mark goes up. His eyebrows lifted and for a moment I saw a grin spread; I half expected a comment in front of his friends. Instead he said, "Thank you, ma'am. I'm glad it's fixed." Then he asked what he should have done to make sure I heard him earlier. We agreed he would bring a written query, and I would reply within the week.

Indu, Science teacher

qa.q: When did Indu find the mistake in Vaibhav's total?
qa.a: In March, while rechecking last term's papers for the moderation meeting.

qa.q: What did Indu notice about Vaibhav's feelings when she told him?
qa.a: A grin began to spread, so he felt vindicated, but he did not gloat. He thanked her and said he was glad it was fixed.

qa.q: What did Vaibhav and Indu agree to so that concerns are raised well in future?
qa.a: He will bring a written query and she will reply within the week.

qa.q: How might Vaibhav see the problem of not being heard in November?
qa.a: He seems to see it partly as something he can help fix, since he asked what he should have done to make sure she heard him earlier.

grounding: Months later a teacher admits a marking error; the student accepts it graciously and asks how to raise concerns better.

passage: Afreen arrived at the club forty minutes early, as always, to watch Coach Jagdish set up cones. Everything he said she wrote in a small notebook: keep your knees soft, look up, move before the ball does. Her footwork got better every week and she glowed when he said her name. Then one Thursday, in the heat, he made a girl who had missed a pass run laps without water and told the team, "Don't mention today's drill at home. Parents don't understand training." Afreen felt a strange cold in her stomach. She wanted his approval more than anything, and she still believed most of what he taught her. But she thought, that isn't right. That evening she told her father exactly what had happened.

qa.q: Where did Afreen write down what Coach Jagdish said?
qa.a: In a small notebook.

qa.q: Why did Afreen feel a strange cold in her stomach on Thursday?
qa.a: Because the coach made a girl run laps without water and told the team not to mention it at home. She still wanted his approval but sensed it was wrong.

qa.q: What would you advise Afreen to do about her coach?
qa.a: Keep learning the footwork and other useful skills but trust her own judgement, and tell a trusted adult like her father or a club official about anything that feels like mistreatment.

qa.q: How might the girl who ran the laps feel about Afreen telling her father?
qa.a: Perhaps relieved that someone spoke up, or worried about trouble. Either way, she was mistreated and told to stay silent, so being backed up could matter to her.

grounding: A player who worships her coach still learns from him but notices a line crossed and does not stay silent.

passage:
"You didn't say a word all the way home," Irfan said on the bus.
"He called me a waste of a jersey. In front of the whole team."
"Again?"
"Tuesday is the worst. My stomach hurts before I even get to the ground."
"Abhinav, extra laps, hard drills, being told your pass was lazy, that's tough training. Being shouted at and shamed until you dread going, that's different."
"But we win because of him."
"Winning doesn't need the shouting."
"And last week he grabbed my arm really hard. It felt wrong."
"Then you tell your mother tonight, and the sports teacher. I'll come with you."
Abhinav looked out at the road and nodded.

qa.q: What did the coach call Abhinav in front of the team?
qa.a: A waste of a jersey.

qa.q: What was Abhinav feeling on Tuesdays before practice, and how can you tell?
qa.a: Dread. His stomach hurt before he even reached the ground.

qa.q: What difference does Irfan draw between tough training and something worse?
qa.a: Extra laps, hard drills and honest feedback are tough training. Shouting and shaming until someone dreads going, or grabbing that feels wrong, is not okay and should be told to a parent or school official.

qa.q: How does Irfan see Abhinav's situation compared with his own view of the coach's results?
qa.a: He accepts that the team wins but insists winning does not need shouting. He offers to go along, so he treats it as serious and wants Abhinav not to face it alone.

grounding: A coach shames players to win; a friend helps distinguish tough training from abuse and urges telling adults.

passage: Emeka had spent every Saturday for a month in the robotics room, wiring the sensors for Wei's entry to the regional contest. Wei, a senior, kept saying, "Great work. When my team is picked, you're in, I promise." But the praise never came with a date or a role. On a rainy Saturday in Manchester, Emeka finally asked, "Will my name be on the entry, and which team am I joining?" Wei laughed it off. "Let's see how it goes." Emeka felt his stomach sink. He'd hoped, and hoping had kept him quiet. That night he emailed Ms Thompson, the club advisor, asking for a chance to work on a project of his own, and asked another student who was willing to share what they knew.

qa.q: What did Emeka spend every Saturday doing for a month?
qa.a: Wiring the sensors for Wei's entry to the regional contest in the robotics room.

qa.q: Why had Emeka stayed quiet for so long, and what changed?
qa.a: He hoped the praise and Wei's promise would turn into a real place on the team. When Wei laughed off his direct question, he saw nothing was being offered and his stomach sank.

qa.q: What would you advise Emeka to do next?
qa.a: Ask clear questions about credit and roles, look for other mentors, and choose projects where his effort is recognised, as he began to do by writing to Ms Thompson.

qa.q: How might Wei see Emeka's question?
qa.a: Possibly as an awkward one, since he laughed it off and avoided a promise. He may not like admitting he was using Emeka's time for his own entry.

grounding: A mentor uses a student's work and time while promising opportunities; the student asks clear questions and seeks other mentors.

passage: I'm Sarita, and I still think about the Tuesday afternoons in Class 9 when Himani ma'am stayed back after school to go through my English essays. She never asked for anything. No gift, no favour, no promise that I'd join her club. When I tried to thank her once, she just said, "Do the same for someone one day." For a long time I thought she was always right. When she suggested I take arts, I almost nodded on reflex. But I loved science, and one afternoon I told her, my heart pounding. She was quiet, then said, "Good. Tell me why." I'm now helping two juniors with their essays. Thanking her was easy. Disagreeing with her was harder, and taught me more.

qa.q: On which afternoons did Himani ma'am stay back to help Sarita?
qa.a: On Tuesday afternoons in Class 9.

qa.q: Why did Sarita almost nod on reflex when Himani ma'am suggested arts?
qa.a: Because she had come to think her mentor was always right. She loved science, though, and her pounding heart shows how hard it was to say so.

qa.q: What could Sarita do to show gratitude for what Himani gave her?
qa.a: Thank her and pass it on, as Himani asked, which Sarita does by helping two juniors with their essays. 🙂

qa.q: How might Himani ma'am have felt when Sarita told her she preferred science?
qa.a: Probably pleased. She stayed quiet, then said, "Good. Tell me why," which suggests she welcomed Sarita thinking for herself.

grounding: A mentor gave time freely; the protagonist thanks her, passes it on and learns she can still disagree.

passage: The rain had turned the pitch to mud, and the final was in forty minutes. Coach Ujjwal read out the starting eleven, and Parveen's name wasn't in it again. She stared at her boots. He always picks Kavya and Nisha, she thought. She wanted to throw her bib down and walk out. But her bus fare was already paid and her mother was coming to watch. Instead, at the interval she went to him. "Coach, what do I need to fix to start?" He looked surprised. "Your first touch under pressure. You panic when the ball arrives." She nodded. "Then I'll stay after practice." Her jaw still felt tight when she came on for the last ten minutes, but she had something to work on.

qa.q: How long before the final was the starting eleven read out?
qa.a: Forty minutes.

qa.q: What did Parveen think and want when her name wasn't in the starting eleven?
qa.a: She thought Coach Ujjwal always picks Kavya and Nisha, and she felt hurt enough to want to throw her bib down and walk out.

qa.q: What small step helped Parveen after being benched?
qa.a: She asked the coach directly what she needed to fix and then planned to stay after practice, instead of quitting angrily or complaining behind his back.

qa.q: How might Coach Ujjwal have felt when Parveen asked her question?
qa.a: Surprised, as his face showed, and probably pleased that she asked. He gave her a specific, honest answer about her first touch.

grounding: A benched player resents the coach but asks what to improve and keeps training instead of quitting or gossiping.

passage:
Supervisor's note, robotics club.

I noticed that Pankaj, a Class 7 student, has begun to copy Hrithik in everything: the same haircut, the same phrases ("no worries, boss"), even the way he holds a soldering iron. Hrithik seemed uncomfortable, rather than pleased. When I asked, he said, "He thinks I never make mistakes." So I suggested he show Pankaj a failed circuit. Yesterday I watched Hrithik open his bin of burnt boards and say, "I ruined all of these. Try it your way first, then compare." Pankaj looked stunned, then a little relieved, and started a design of his own. I will keep an eye on it. They have both been invited to present at the fair.

qa.q: What phrase has Pankaj copied from Hrithik?
qa.a: "No worries, boss".

qa.q: What was Hrithik feeling about Pankaj's copying, and what did he say that shows it?
qa.a: He seemed uncomfortable, not pleased. He said, "He thinks I never make mistakes," which suggests he felt the admiration was unrealistic.

qa.q: What could Hrithik keep doing to be a good example?
qa.a: Admit his flaws openly, as he did with the burnt boards, and encourage Pankaj to try his own way first.

qa.q: What might it be like for Pankaj to see his idol's failed circuits?
qa.a: Startling at first, since he looked stunned, but also a relief. It shows him that even a person he admires makes mistakes, so he can try his own designs without fear.

grounding: An older student is idolised by a younger one, admits his flaws and encourages the younger to think for himself.

passage:
I saw it behind the canteen, so I'm writing down what I remember. Three of Imran's friends were passing round a vape. One of them held it out. "Come on, one puff. Don't be boring." Imran smiled, not nervously as far as I could tell, though I can't say what was going on inside him. "I'm boring, fine," he said lightly. "Not for me." They pushed again and one rolled his eyes. Imran just shrugged, said, "I'm going to the library, coming?" and walked off. Two of them shouted something after him. I'm not sure whether he was upset. Later he sat with me at lunch and talked about cricket as if nothing had happened.

Parveen, Class 10

qa.q: Where did Parveen see the friends offering Imran a vape?
qa.a: Behind the canteen.

qa.q: What does Imran's manner suggest about how he handled the pressure, and how sure can Parveen be?
qa.a: He smiled, spoke lightly and left, so he seems steady and unwilling to give in. But Parveen admits she can't know what he felt inside.

qa.q: What could Imran do if the friends keep pushing him?
qa.a: Keep his light, steady no, keep walking away and spend time with people who don't put his safety at risk. If it gets worse, he can tell an adult he trusts.

qa.q: How might one of the friends see Imran's refusal?
qa.a: Possibly as a small sting. One rolled his eyes and two shouted after Imran, so they may feel rejected or embarrassed that he wasn't swayed.

grounding: An observer describes a friend who is called boring, says a light steady no and leaves.
